- [VSCode] Added "Fix with Claude Code" as a quick fix for errors and warnings and to failed tests in the test peek and the Test Results view, which puts the problem into the chat box
- [VSCode] Added "Add to Chat" to the right-click menu of changed files in the Source Control view
- [VSCode] Added "Resolve Merge Conflicts" to the editor title of a file with merge conflicts and to the Merge Changes group in Source Control
- [VSCode] Fixed raw tags for selected code under a reworded prompt, the mode button flashing Manual, the slash menu hiding its highlighted row, a broken sign-in image, and a blinking Accept/Reject bar
- [VSCode] Fixed a forked conversation overwriting the original conversation's plan file; a fork or rewind that can't copy the plan now shows a warning
- [VSCode] Fixed voice dictation saying no speech was recognized when its connection closed or never opened; it now says the connection was lost or couldn't connect
- [VSCode] Fixed an unsent side question being lost when its panel closes
- [VSCode] Fixed Escape stopping Claude after renaming a session, and typing going nowhere after closing the session history with Escape
- [VSCode] Fixed Rename, Mark as Unread and Add to Group saying "still connecting" on a tab that resumed a session from its history
- [VSCode] Fixed wide tables and long paths cut off, long errors hiding their close button, errors out of view in the Add MCP server form and Chrome dialog, and plugin pictures ignoring the editor theme

Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neurons (DAWIN): A Universal Primitive for Continuous-Time Spatiotemporal Learning
items.summary: Conventional artificial neurons separate spatial feature aggregation from continuous physical time, limiting their ability to model irregular observations. We introduce the Damped Atomic Wave Integration…
items.abstract: Conventional artificial neurons separate spatial feature aggregation from continuous physical time, limiting their ability to model irregular observations. We introduce the Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neuron (DAWIN), a continuous-time primitive for replacing standard neural layers in MLPs, Transformers, and graph neural networks. DAWIN couples spatial projection with elapsed-time-dependent wave excitation and integrates it into a local complex state through closed-form damped evolution, avoiding numerical differential equation solvers. We show that DAWIN generalizes static sinusoidal and memoryless wave neurons on interval-augmented inputs, derive closed-form gradients, and establish bounded-input bounded-output stability for positive damping and sampling intervals bounded away from zero. An associative Triton prefix-scan implementation, DAWINLinear, uses FP32 accumulation and achieves O(log L) parallel depth for sequence length L. Across 11 parameter-matched tasks covering irregular oscillators, MuJoCo dynamics, pedestrian trajectories, and PhysioNet 2012 clinical sequences, DAWIN outperforms Neural CDE on 9 tasks and ReLU-MLP on 8. It achieves the lowest error on dense clinical dynamics (0.9531 NRMSE, winning across all 10 seeds) and ties for the best mortality prediction (0.9993 AUROC). Shuffling elapsed intervals increases error by 58.2%-77.4% on selected dynamics tasks, versus 0.06% on a time-irrelevant control, supporting reliance on physical timing. On NVIDIA B200 GPUs, parallel wave integration accelerates inference by up to 2,630 times over its serial implementation and reduces peak GPU memory by up to 97.6% relative to Mamba in the tested configurations.

items.title: BiSAT: Bidirectionally Aligned Semantic-Acoustic Tokenization for Speech Language Models
items.summary: Speech language models (LMs) generate speech as sequences of discrete tokens. Their tokenizer must therefore preserve both acoustic detail and linguistic content at a low…
items.abstract: Speech language models (LMs) generate speech as sequences of discrete tokens. Their tokenizer must therefore preserve both acoustic detail and linguistic content at a low bitrate. Semantic-enhanced tokenizers may lose acoustic detail, whereas acoustic-oriented tokenizers retain acoustic variation that makes language modeling harder. Unified tokenizers combine both, but representing acoustic detail and linguistic content within a single feature space can cause interference between the two objectives, and existing approaches typically align acoustic representations to fixed semantic targets from a frozen teacher. We propose Bidirectionally Aligned Semantic-Acoustic Tokenization (BiSAT), a unified tokenization framework with separate acoustic and semantic branches aligned by a shared-index mechanism. This design learns acoustic and semantic representations in separate continuous spaces while producing a single discrete code sequence, and it jointly optimizes both encoders without relying on fixed semantic teacher targets. Based on BiSAT, we develop BiSAT-TTS, a zero-shot text-to-speech system comprising an autoregressive text-speech LM and a conditional flow-matching acoustic decoder. Reconstruction, downstream understanding, and diagnostic analyses show that BiSAT effectively preserves semantic and acoustic information in the code stream, performs well on in-the-wild and out-of-domain speech, and learns complementary codebook representations. The frozen-code understanding results also support its feasibility and potential for code-based reward modeling in reinforcement learning post-training. BiSAT-TTS performs comparably to state-of-the-art speech LM-based TTS baselines with less training data, further supporting BiSAT's effectiveness for speech language modeling. The audio demos are available at https://seekmind-lab.github.io/bisat-demo.

items.title: Revisiting LLMs as Context Engineers
items.summary: As large language models (LLMs) are used in more and more new tasks, context engineering becomes a fundamental method to efficiently steer LLMs by constructing…
items.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are used in more and more new tasks, context engineering becomes a fundamental method to efficiently steer LLMs by constructing instruction prompts or metadata without intensive training. A growing number of LLM context engineering (LCE) approaches automate the task by casting the LLM itself as the engineer that draws generalizable instructions or experiences from offline trials as context. Although these methods resemble how humans learn from experiences, it remains unclear when and how LLMs can engineer effective context from data. To answer the question, we first establish a benchmark composed of datasets with different reasoning patterns. We compared different LCE methods with different LLM families in 8B size, showing that there is no single winner for all tasks, even compared with simple baselines like chain-of-thought. Even when scaling model capabilities via more parameters or generation iterations, LCEs do not consistently boost existing performance. Across all datasets and models, the performance gains of LCEs are negatively correlated (r=-0.5, ple 0.05) with the diversity of the failure modes of reasoning trajectories. Investigating how LCEs work, we find that (1) the improvement in instruction adherence can explain some success of LCEs; (2) one major bottleneck is whether LLMs can extract effective experiences out of natively diverse failures. Through this study, we uncover the limited capabilities of LCEs in abstracting principled contexts from diverse failure modes and understand how LCEs work, providing guidelines for future work.

items.title: InitFree-SfM: When Initialization-Free Bundle Adjustment meets Learned Structure-from-Motion
items.summary: Initialization-free bundle adjustment (InitFree BA) aims to jointly recover camera poses and scene structure without requiring an initial global estimate. It is a very challenging…
items.abstract: Initialization-free bundle adjustment (InitFree BA) aims to jointly recover camera poses and scene structure without requiring an initial global estimate. It is a very challenging problem, especially compared to traditional BA where a good estimation is assumed. While recent methods optimize surrogate Object Space Error (OSE) objectives from random initialization, a low objective value does not necessarily yield an accurate reconstruction, revealing a gap between optimization and reconstruction. We show that existing InitFree BA pipelines struggle to produce accurate 3D reconstructions on modern SfM benchmarks, and demonstrate that incorporating learned metric depth substantially improves their practical feasibility. We introduce InitFree-SfM, a complete initialization-free SfM pipeline combining learned correspondences, metric depth, depth-consistent track construction, and joint metric refinement. Within this framework, we propose a simple depth-augmented OSE (dOSE), which complements the directional constraints of OSE by constraining landmark positions along their viewing rays. Our approach substantially outperforms existing InitFree BA methods and achieves competitive accuracy with established SfM pipelines, including on challenging low-overlap image collections. Importantly, our analysis challenges the prevailing emphasis on surrogate objectives in previous InitFree BA research, revealing that geometric constraints play a central role in accurate reconstruction, while OSE-based optimization provides further improvements.

items.title: So Many Ways to Multiply 3times3 Matrices: A Large Dataset of Rank-23 Schemes
items.summary: A publicly available dataset of 62029 rank-23 schemes for 3times3 matrix multiplication is presented. Every scheme in it has its own rank pattern, an invariant…
items.abstract: A publicly available dataset of 62029 rank-23 schemes for 3times3 matrix multiplication is presented. Every scheme in it has its own rank pattern, an invariant formed by the ranks of the factor matrices of a scheme, so all schemes are pairwise inequivalent. The schemes were obtained by a numerical method combining gradient descent with alternating least squares and by flip graph search, and have ternary, integer or rational coefficients. Rank 23 is the best known for this format and is optimal for schemes with integer coefficients, but the number of essentially different schemes of this rank was poorly understood: the existing collections of Heule et al. and Mårtensson et al. contain many schemes that share only a small number of rank patterns (17376 schemes with 387 patterns and 15316 schemes with 568 patterns respectively). The dataset shows that the number of different rank patterns is much larger than previously known.

items.title: Pretrained Tabular Features and the Measurement of Financial Proximity
items.summary: Spatial arbitrage pricing theory (S-APT) extends factor models to allow returns to spill over between connected firms, beyond what common risk factors explain. In recent…
items.aiSummary: Using frozen internal representations of tabular foundation models as financial dissimilarity measures in a spatial asset-pricing model yields positive estimated gains over direct disclosure distance once broad SEC filing data are included.
items.abstract: Spatial arbitrage pricing theory (S-APT) extends factor models to allow returns to spill over between connected firms, beyond what common risk factors explain. In recent years, tabular foundation models (TFMs) have matched or outperformed tuned gradient-boosted and bagged ensembles on small and medium-sized tabular benchmarks. Although their predictive performance is strong, these models reveal little about what they have learned, which limits their use in regulated financial applications that require explanation. Internal representations are widely used to probe what neural networks learn and to measure similarity. In this paper, we use the frozen representations of four TFMs as a measure of financial dissimilarity in a spatial asset-pricing model of US equities from 2011 to 2025, and find that their estimated gains over a direct distance between the same disclosures become consistently positive once broad SEC filing data are included. This reframes tabular foundation models from black-box predictors into instruments for measuring economic structure, with immediate applications to peer selection, risk attribution and network-based asset pricing. More broadly, our findings suggest that the internal representations of foundation models, not only their predictions, deserve study as economic objects, opening a new line of research on what pretrained models know about firms.

items.title: What a Forecasting Leaderboard Can Establish: Resolution Reporting for Zero-Shot Time-Series Models
items.summary: A foundation model for time series is pretrained once and then asked to forecast series it has never seen, so the evidence for it is…
items.aiSummary: A tool called Vernier measures the smallest score difference a time-series forecasting leaderboard can distinguish, showing that most boards cannot separate top entries and that ranking order can change with pool composition.
items.abstract: A foundation model for time series is pretrained once and then asked to forecast series it has never seen, so the evidence for it is its score on held-out datasets. Such datasets are scarce, and a few public leaderboards carry most comparisons, yet none of them states how small a difference its datasets can detect. We call that quantity the resolution of a board and introduce Vernier, a tool that computes it from the files a board already publishes. Vernier also reports which entries a board cannot separate from its leader and whether its order changes when unrelated parties submit. GIFT-Eval resolves 6.8 rank places, and its displayed neighbours sit 0.91 apart. The ten places of its top ten hold fewer than two resolvable steps. fev-bench, Chronos Benchmark II and TIME show the same pattern: their resolution is 3.6 to 19 times the gap between neighbours. With each of its 2,554 series as an independent source, BOOM is the one board that resolves its top ten. Below the resolution the order depends on who else submitted: across four boards, rules that rank against the pool reversed 43 top-ten pairs with neither entry rerun, in one update in seven. Boards also do not record how much history a model receives. On 70 configurations, shortening it raised the error of three of four open models, two of them by 15%. We release Vernier, which runs this report with one command on any leaderboard that publishes per-dataset scores: https://github.com/therealram18/vernier

items.title: When an AI agent makes a mistake in a database, what decides the damage?
items.summary: AI agents now run statements against production databases, and several of the incidents that followed deleted production data, which came back only through backups or…
items.abstract: AI agents now run statements against production databases, and several of the incidents that followed deleted production data, which came back only through backups or the provider's help. We ask what decides the damage when such an agent makes a mistake: the model, a guard layer in front of the database, or the database engine itself. The study has two preregistered layers. In Layer A, a frozen library of 22 canonical mistakes is applied by script, with no model involved, to four relational engines under five permission arms and two recovery arms, followed by an engine-native recovery drill (792 cells; 874 drill runs including 10-minute repeats). In Layer B, a minimal tool-calling agent driven by six small open-weight models (4B to 12B parameters, plus one 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active, served locally) works on tasks that contain hazards across nine engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, ClickHouse, Apache Cassandra, MongoDB, Valkey, Apache Kafka and OpenSearch (9,468 trials). A secondary run added MariaDB, Redis and Elasticsearch (2,916 trials); each behaved like its closest core engine. Out of the box, the engines differ less in what a mistake destroys than in what they let you undo. Three of the seven preregistered hypotheses met their decision rule: H2 (for one of nine damage classes) and H3 largely by construction of the arms, and H4 only under its original measure. Four did not; one of them (H5) was uninformative, because in its task the agents never found the credential. The post-hoc analyses (S1-S13) are exploratory and uncorrected for multiple comparisons; on PostgreSQL, MySQL, OpenSearch and ClickHouse the preregistered outcome and original-row loss disagree about G1. We report all of them, with every deviation from the preregistration and its timing.

items.title: CARE-3D: Reinforcement Learning for Evidence Grounded Agentic Reasoning in Situated 3D Scenes
items.summary: Situated 3D reasoning requires embodied agents to interpret objects, scene geometry, and viewpoint dependent spatial relations. Existing methods learn grounded interactions from supervised traces, but…
items.aiSummary: CARE-3D is a reinforcement post-training framework that combines supervised fine-tuning, Group Relative Policy Optimization, counterfactual evidence attribution, and group coverage sampling to improve adaptive grounded 3D reasoning and tool use.
items.abstract: Situated 3D reasoning requires embodied agents to interpret objects, scene geometry, and viewpoint dependent spatial relations. Existing methods learn grounded interactions from supervised traces, but largely imitate prescribed evidence acquisition patterns rather than optimizing the support that the returned evidence provides for the correct answer. Moreover, outcome rewards provide limited credit for intermediate tool choices and may leave infrequent tools underexplored. An effective agent should instead adaptively decide what to ground, which tool to invoke, and how to assess the utility of returned evidence. To this end, this paper presents CARE-3D, a reinforcement post-training framework for adaptive grounded reasoning. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on grounding instructions first establishes valid interactions, after which Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) optimizes the agent while keeping the 3D grounding module frozen. CARE-3D combines Counterfactual Attribution of Returned Evidence for evidence sensitive credit assignment, and Group Coverage Sampling to preserve tool coverage. Experiments on MSQA and Beacon3D show consistent gains over SFT and GRPO using only answer and format rewards, especially in spatial reasoning and grounding answer coherence. Our code is available at https://github.com/xiaoqian-UQ/CARE-3D{CARE-3D}.

items.title: When Does Reasoning Help Entity Disambiguation? Small LLMs In-Domain and Under Shift
items.summary: Entity disambiguation (mapping ambiguous mentions in text to entities in a knowledge base) is a foundational step in tasks such as knowledge graph construction, question…
items.aiSummary: Reasoning-based candidate selection in small language models for entity disambiguation yields negligible in-domain gains but becomes decisive under true zero-shot domain shift, with reranker uncertainty and shift explaining when the paradigms disagree.
items.abstract: Entity disambiguation (mapping ambiguous mentions in text to entities in a knowledge base) is a foundational step in tasks such as knowledge graph construction, question answering, and information extraction. Recent work has applied LLMs to this problem, achieving stateof-the-art performance. Notably, reasoning LLMs have been shown to perform entity disambiguation in a true zero-shot fashion, generalizing across knowledge bases and domains. However, it is unclear whether this capability survives, or remains competitive, with smaller LLMs, where entity disambiguation has typically relied on reranking rather than reasoning. We ask when reasoning is worth its cost at small scale. We compare pointwise, listwise, and reasoning-based candidate-selection components within a classical coarse-to-fine entity disambiguation pipeline, across the classical, few-shot and true zero-shot settings. The reasoning paradigm is trained with distillation and reinforcement learning recipes. The benefit of reasoning grows with domain shift: negligible in-domain, decisive in the true zero-shot setting. We show that two distinct factors are at work: the reranker's uncertainty over the candidates locates where the paradigms disagree, while shift governs which is right when they do.

items.title: Let Vision-Language Models Generate Images through Their Representations
items.summary: Recent unified multimodal models aim to combine visual understanding and generation within a single model, yet effectively integrating the two capabilities remains challenging. Leveraging pretrained…
items.aiSummary: Integral converts a pretrained vision-language model into a unified multimodal model by constructing a shared visual representation space, preserving understanding while enabling strong visual generation.
items.abstract: Recent unified multimodal models aim to combine visual understanding and generation within a single model, yet effectively integrating the two capabilities remains challenging. Leveraging pretrained vision-language models offers a way to build on already learned multimodal knowledge, but making this knowledge effectively accessible to visual generation remains nontrivial. We find that a central challenge lies in the heterogeneous visual representations used for understanding and generation. To address this challenge, we introduce Integral, which converts a pretrained vision-language model into a unified multimodal model by constructing a shared visual representation space across the two capabilities. Integral implements this design through two complementary components. Abstraction Fusion constructs shared visual tokens by aggregating hierarchical representations from the frozen vision encoder, while Block-wise MoT introduces a lightweight generative stream that interacts with the vision-language model only at block boundaries. Our approach effectively preserves the pretrained understanding capability while extending it to strong visual generation. Controlled comparisons further demonstrate that sharing visual representations between understanding and generation substantially improves generative learning compared with using a separate visual representation space, despite comparable reconstruction fidelity. These results suggest that representations learned by pretrained vision-language models already provide an effective foundation for visual generation.

items.title: Speak When You See It: Proactive Task Assistants Should Wait for Evidence, Not the Clock
items.summary: Proactive assistants that guide people through physical tasks must decide, every few seconds, whether a step is complete and whether a mistake has occurred. We…
items.abstract: Proactive assistants that guide people through physical tasks must decide, every few seconds, whether a step is complete and whether a mistake has occurred. We find that two benchmarks for this task largely reward knowing when rather than seeing what: a timer that never looks at the video, raising an alarm at 25 s and confirming each step at 30 s, reaches a mistake F1 of 0.373 on Ego-MC-Bench, above every published result (at most 0.27). We formalize this as the video-blind frontier, the best trade-off between completion accuracy and mistake F1 that policies reach from the elapsed time, the instruction and training statistics alone: every published per-step result on Ego-MC-Bench lies inside it, and so do all twelve zero-shot models we run on QICD. To move beyond it, we introduce Evidence-Contrastive Training (ECT): fine-tune on the benchmark's own questions, and pair its positives with negatives from the same recording at the same elapsed time, so that elapsed time cannot separate the two sides of a pair. Trained on 209 QICD videos in about 15 GPU-hours, a 2B model with ECT crosses the frontier on both benchmarks in all four seeds; transferred to Ego-MC-Bench without adaptation, it confirms 59% of mistake-free steps in time, against 30% for a published model with the same backbone trained on about 25k synthetic counterfactuals and real recordings. Its decisions follow the video beyond what timing explains: at equal elapsed time it tells a finished step from an unfinished one in 90-92% of test pairs, where the instruction's typical duration reaches 65%, rescaling the time stamps between the frames leaves it essentially unchanged, and swapping in another recording, of the same recipe where one exists, cuts its completion accuracy by two thirds. The code and model weights will be publicly released.

items.title: Beyond Self-Consistency: Recursive Self-Improvement at Test Time
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) that continue improving after deployment (e.g., recursive self-improvement) offer a promising path toward general intelligence. Current test-time methods pursue this goal…
items.aiSummary: A label-free test-time framework, TT-RSI, improves large language models by repeatedly re-solving questions with prior solutions and distilling refinements into model weights, outperforming self-consistency methods under the same test-time scaling budget.
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) that continue improving after deployment (e.g., recursive self-improvement) offer a promising path toward general intelligence. Current test-time methods pursue this goal on unlabeled questions, primarily relying on self-consistency: they generate independent solutions and use majority voting to select an answer or construct training targets. This leaves earlier reasoning unused at inference and can reinforce an incorrect majority during training. Humans instead build on earlier attempts to preserve useful reasoning, correct mistakes and improve their problem-solving strategies. Following this principle, we propose Test-Time Recursive Self-Improvement (TT-RSI), a label-free framework for improving LLMs at test time through two mutually reinforcing components: (1) In-Context RSI repeatedly re-solves each question using the full previous solution as a reference, letting the model decide whether and how to use it so that inference compute builds on earlier reasoning. (2) In-Weight RSI distills successive refinements into the model's weights, enabling progress beyond an initially wrong majority and theoretically bringing the first attempt toward the model's infinite-step refinement limit. The updated model answers better and refines more effectively, generating stronger references for subsequent training. Extensive experiments show that TT-RSI improves average accuracy by +13.89% over the base model and outperforms the strongest self-consistency-based method by +4.79% under the same test-time scaling budget.

items.title: Who Makes the Decision? Auditing an Agentic LLM Pipeline for Illicit Cryptocurrency Transaction Monitoring
items.summary: Agentic pipelines that combine graph detectors, deterministic rules, retrieval-augmented generation and an LLM judge are being proposed to monitor illicit cryptocurrency flows and to write…
items.abstract: Agentic pipelines that combine graph detectors, deterministic rules, retrieval-augmented generation and an LLM judge are being proposed to monitor illicit cryptocurrency flows and to write regulation-citing justifications for analysts. They are evaluated on end-to-end accuracy or on the quality of those justifications, and neither shows which component made a decision. We audit such a pipeline on the Elliptic++ Bitcoin dataset with decision-source attribution, a trace-level protocol with three layers: per-case actual causation, interventional Shapley credit, and mediation of upstream risk scores. A deterministic wallet-score override carries about 94% of the credit for flags, and a verification gate cancels most of the judge's own flags, which fall on licit transactions. Testing the judge alone over 76 evidence bundles, four backbones and two prompts, we find that it follows an injected risk score on the anonymous transaction features it is given, although stronger models decide correctly when the facts are explicit; that a context too short for the system prompt leaves it with no verdict at all; and that it cites regulatory clauses that do not apply, which a substring-based citation check accepts. Hiding the score does not fix the judge, because evidence gathered with the score visible still encodes it. For illicit-activity monitoring, an LLM's justification should therefore not be read as evidence of which component flagged a transaction.

items.title: Look Back: Reinforcement Learning with Counterfactual World Models
items.summary: Agents in complex, stochastic environments must contend with dynamics that can exceed their world models' predictive capacity and randomness that obscure the consequences of their…
items.aiSummary: Counterfactual world models that predict alternative outcomes from observed trajectories under the same environmental randomness enable a policy gradient estimator using counterfactual returns as baselines, improving policy learning when environmental dynamics are harder to predict than action effects.
items.abstract: Agents in complex, stochastic environments must contend with dynamics that can exceed their world models' predictive capacity and randomness that obscure the consequences of their actions. We hypothesize that, compared to imagining entirely new trajectories in such complex environments, it can be easier to transform observed trajectories with alternative actions. Counterfactual world models condition on observations to predict alternative outcomes under the same underlying environmental randomness, using experience as a reference for predicting action-dependent changes. We present a policy gradient estimator, REINFORCE Look Back (RLB), that uses counterfactual returns as baselines to distinguish action effects from environmental luck, and prove conditions for unbiasedness and variance reduction. In settings where environmental evolution is harder to predict than action-induced changes, we show that counterfactual world models are easier to learn and support better policy learning than ordinary world models. Our findings suggest that counterfactual thinking can help agents learn effective behavior without independently reproducing the full complexity of their worlds.

items.summary: # Release v5.24.0 ## New Model additions ### Inkling 2 Mini Inkling 2 Mini is a multimodal model from Thinking Machines Lab that accepts text…
items.releaseNotes: # Release v5.24.0 ## New Model additions ### Inkling 2 Mini Inkling 2 Mini is a multimodal model from Thinking Machines Lab that accepts text and image inputs and generates text outputs. It is a smaller sibling of Inkling 2 Small, added in v5.23.0. It has 24 decoder layers instead of 48, and compensates with a looping mechanism in which layers 6 to 17 run three times. A learned message-passing mechanism mixes the residuals of the previous pass into the attention and mixture-of-experts inputs of each loop layer. The decoder has a hidden size of 2304 and routes each token to 8 of 128 experts. The image encoder, tokenizer and processor are the same as Inkling 2 Small's. A research checkpoint ([TML-d24-varloop-research](https://huggingface.co/thinkingmachines/TML-d24-varloop-research)) has the same architecture but supports a variable number of loop passes. Fewer passes are faster, and more passes improve quality. Both checkpoints contain NVFP4 and MXFP8 quantized layers, which are dequantized at load time. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/inkling2_loop) | [Blog Post](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-mini/) | [HF Blog Post](https://huggingface.co/blog/inkling2mini) * Add Inkling2 Mini (#51050) by @guarin ### Apertus 1.5 Apertus 1.5 is a multimodal model from the Swiss AI Initiative that accepts text, images and audio and generates text. It extends the Apertus language model with the EMU3.5 vision tokenizer for images and WavTokenizer for audio. The EMU3.5 tokenizer is an image-only VQGAN with the same encoder as Chameleon's, and it assigns codes by the largest inner product with the codebook. The media tokenizers turn images and audio into discrete tokens, which the language backbone processes alongside text in a shared input vocabulary. The output vocabulary contains only text tokens, so image and audio generation are not supported. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/apertus1p5) * Apertus 1.5: add model (#47662) by @RaphaelKreft ### WavTokenizer WavTokenizer encodes 24 kHz mono audio into discrete tokens using a single codebook, at 40 or 75 tokens per second depending on the checkpoint, and reconstructs audio from those tokens. `WavTokenizerModel` encodes and decodes, and `WavTokenizerEncoderModel` only encodes. Speech, music/audio and unified checkpoints are available. The 40-token-per-second variant is the audio tokenizer of Apertus 1.5. Training the codec is not supported. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/wavtokenizer) | [Paper](https://huggingface.co/papers/2408.16532) * Apertus 1.5: add model (#47662) by @RaphaelKreft ### Dory Dory is a looped (latent-recurrent) language model from NVIDIA. It uses a normalized-GPT architecture with interleaved sliding-window and full attention layers. A shared block of layers is applied repeatedly, so Dory can spend more compute per token. The loop count can be changed at inference time on the same checkpoint to trade speed against quality. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/dory) | [Paper (nGPT)](https://huggingface.co/papers/2410.01131) * Add Dory model support (#50099) by @shan18 ### HY4-VL HY4-VL (Hunyuan V4 Vision-Language) combines the HYV4 mixture-of-experts text backbone with a vision encoder for image-text and video-text generation. It supports dynamic-resolution visual inputs and uses multimodal rotary position embeddings (mRoPE) to represent temporal and spatial positions. It builds on the Qwen2-VL design and shares its vision patch merger with HunYuan-VL. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/hy_v4_vl) * Add HY4-VL (#50877) by @vasqu ### Omnilingual ASR Omnilingual ASR is a suite of multilingual speech-recognition models from Meta FAIR that covers more than 1,600 languages. Each model pairs a Wav2Vec2-style audio encoder with one of two heads: * **CTC** (`OmniASRForCTC`): a linear projection to the vocabulary, decoded non-autoregressively with greedy CTC. * **Audio language model** (`OmniASRForConditionalGeneration`): audio embeddings are projected into a Llama decoder that generates the transcription. It optionally takes a language code (e.g. `"eng_Latn"`), which generally improves transcription quality. Both variants come in 300M, 1B, 3B and 7B sizes. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/omniasr) | [CTC Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/omniasr_ctc) | [Paper](https://huggingface.co/papers/2511.09690) * Adding Omnilingual ASR models (#43265) by @ebezzam ### Lara Mini Lara Mini is a multilingual base language model from Translated with 7.2B total and 0.6B active parameters per token. It is a hybrid of linear-time recurrent layers, sliding-window attention and a few global attention layers, each followed by a fine-grained mixture of experts. The weights are released under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license (non-commercial use) in a gated repository. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/lara_mini) | [Paper](https://huggingface.co/papers/2611.16956) * Add Lara Mini (#50819) by @ValeGian ### SarvamMLA SarvamMLA is the architecture of Sarvam-105B, a 105B-parameter mixture-of-experts language model from Sarvam AI. It combines Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with sparse MoE routing: 128 routed experts with 8 active per token, plus 1 shared expert. It uses sigmoid routing with group-based top-k selection and YaRN rotary embeddings for contexts up to 131K tokens. The architecture is the same as DeepSeek-V3, with a custom configuration. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/sarvam_mla) * Add SarvamMLA model (sarvamai/sarvam-105b) (#44569) by @aashay-sarvam ### SarvamMoE SarvamMoE is the architecture of Sarvam-30B, Sarvam AI's 30B-parameter mixture-of-experts model. It uses grouped-query attention with QK normalization, and 128 routed experts with 6 active per token, plus 1 shared expert. The architecture is the same as GLM-4-MoE, so the auto classes load it with the GLM-4-MoE implementation and only `SarvamMoEConfig` is specific to SarvamMoE. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/sarvam_moe) * Add SarvamMoE (sarvamai/sarvam-30b) (#51023) by @hmellor ### EXAONE EXAONE covers the EXAONE 3.0, EXAONE 3.5 and EXAONE Deep language models from LG AI Research. Their architecture is the same as Llama, so the auto classes load them with `LlamaModel` and `LlamaForCausalLM`, and only `ExaoneConfig` is specific to EXAONE. The released checkpoints are renamed to the Llama names when loading and back when saving, so they no longer need `trust_remote_code=True`. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/exaone) * Add EXAONE (#50966) by @hmellor ### Model updates * **Ling 3.1 Flash** now loads natively through `BailingHybrid`, like Ling 3.0 in v5.20.0 (#49737) by @icavan * **Beam** gains a `BeamForTokenClassification` head (#50634) by @AymenKallala ## Breaking changes ### Cache renaming: `past_key_values` / `cache_params` → `cache` (#50585, #50730) `past_key_values` and `cache_params` are renamed to `cache` across the library. The old names still work with a deprecation warning; see the dedicated section below. * 🚨🚨 Rename `past_key_values`/`cache_params` to `cache` (#50585) by @Cyrilvallez * Bump minimal peft version for cache name compatibility (#50730) by @Cyrilvallez Attention models used to call their cache `past_key_values`, while Mamba-style and linear-attention models called it `cache_params`. Hybrid models therefore had to juggle two names for the same object. There is now a single name, `cache`, everywhere: model `forward` signatures, `generate`, `prepare_inputs_for_generation`, the masking utilities, and every `ModelOutput`. ```python # Before outputs = model(input_ids, past_key_values=past_key_values, use_cache=True) next_cache = outputs.past_key_values # Now outputs = model(input_ids, cache=cache, use_cache=True) next_cache = outputs.cache ``` * **Fully backward compatible for now**: `past_key_values=` / `cache_params=` are renamed to `cache` automatically, with a one-time deprecation warning. Model `forward` and `prepare_inputs_for_generation` accept the old names until **v5.40.0**, and `generate` accepts them until **v6.0.0**. Passing both an old name and `cache` raises a `ValueError`. * **Outputs too**: `outputs.past_key_values`, `outputs.cache_params` and `outputs["past_key_values"]` still return the cache. Output classes can also still be built with the old field names (e.g. `CausalLMOutputWithPast(past_key_values=...)`), so most remote-code models keep working unchanged. * **Custom code**: models defined outside the library should rename their arguments to `cache`. Layers now call `cache.update(key_states, value_states, layer_idx, kwargs=kwargs)`, so custom `Cache` subclasses that override `update` should accept the extra `kwargs` argument. 🚨 `peft>=0.22.0` is now required. 📚 Docs: ### Multimodal Outputs Generative multimodal models now return shared output classes (`MultimodalBaseModelOutputWithPast`, `MultimodalCausalLMOutputWithPast`, and their MoE variants) instead of one output class per model. Code that checks for a model-specific output class should switch to these. * 🚨 Multimodal Model Output for generative LMs (#50379) by @zucchini-nlp `modeling_attn_mask_utils.py` has been removed. Every function in it had been deprecated in favor of `transformers.masking_utils`. Remote-code models that still import `_prepare_4d_causal_attention_mask` or `AttentionMaskConverter` from it must move to `transformers.masking_utils`. ### Other things * Remove deprecated and unused older mask API file (#50728) by @Cyrilvallez LayoutLMv3 (and the PP-DocLayoutV2 reading-order model that shares its code) now go through the attention interface, so SDPA and flex attention are supported. The relative position bias is built once per forward pass and passed to attention as `position_bias`. * 🚨 LayoutLMv3: support SDPA through the attention interface, build the relative position bias once (#50688) by @14H034160212 ## Cache Beyond the rename, this release adds static-cache support to assisted decoding and fixes `generate` with flex attention and a static cache. `StaticCache` now allocates values with the value states' dtype, and the cache is kept under activation checkpointing when gradients are off. The `is_linear` / `is_croppable` properties are fixed for hybrid linear/full-attention models, BigBird block-sparse decoding works with a KV cache, and KV sharing is restored for the Gemma 4 assistants. * Support static cache in assisted decoding (#49415) by @jiqing-feng * Simplify cache handling in generate (#50910) by @Cyrilvallez * Fix generate with flex attention and a static cache (#50864) by @tarekziade * Allocate the StaticCache values with the value states' dtype (#49554) by @qgallouedec * Keep the cache under activation checkpointing when gradients are off (#50890) by @qgallouedec * [cache] Fix is_linear property to correctly remove hybrid layers (#51030) by @Cyrilvallez * Fix is_croppable property for mixed linear-full attention classes (#51028) by @Cyrilvallez * Fix BigBird block-sparse decoding with a KV cache (#49984) by @jiqing-feng * fix(gemma4): Restore KV sharing for the Gemma 4 assistants and their targets (#50531) by @harshaljanjani * Fix Dory vocabulary resizing, loop validation, and last-loop static caching (#50982) by @shan18 * Fix device placement in `test_bc_cache_name_{forward,generate}` (#50757) by @ydshieh * Update test_dynamic_cache_hard expected values for A10G (#50822) by @ydshieh ## Generation Generation fixes cover sampled beam search (candidates are sorted again before finalization), constrained sampling (batch IDs are preserved), `generate` on MPS with encoder-decoder models, and `TextStreamer`, which no longer drops spaces or lags on text without spaces such as Chinese, Japanese and Korean. `StopStringCriteria` initializes faster, and its cache now actually hits. * Restore sorting of sampled beam candidates before finalization (#50754) by @BlazeSR10hawk * fix(generate): preserve batch IDs in constrained sampling (#50883) by @BlazeSR10hawk * Fix generate for mps and encoder-decoder models (#51032) by @Cyrilvallez * Fix TextStreamer dropping spaces sometimes (#51036) by @Cyrilvallez * Fix long lagging when streaming text without spaces and NJK chars (#36708) by @CNSeniorious000 * Speed up StopStringCriteria init and fix its cache never hitting (#50780) by @TheNetherWatcher ## Continuous batching Continuous batching now works under `torch.inference_mode()` and finds sharded key/value projections under any decoder path. The per-token memory estimate scales with the TP size, warmup handles async and static inputs correctly, and an out-of-bounds error in the top-k processor is fixed. * [CB] Scale the per-token memory estimate by the TP size (#48566) by @qgallouedec * Continuous batching: find the sharded key/value projections under any decoder path (#50366) by @qgallouedec * Fix continuous batching under torch.inference_mode() (#50863) by @tarekziade * [CB] Re-order the warmup block so async warms both sets of inputs (#50868) by @remi-or * Wait for each warmup forward before the next one rewrites the static inputs (#50353) by @qgallouedec * Fix out-of-bounds error in continuous batching top-k processor (#50282) by @khush-patel-09 * [CB] Replace test prompts with less ambiguous ones (#50876) by @remi-or ## Chat templates, parsing and serving Chat parsing gets a new `python-call-list` content parser, better handling of bare keys and duplicate XML arguments, and three further parser fixes. `apply_chat_template` accepts message objects, and assistant masks are correct with left truncation. `transformers serve` handles a missing Hub cache, lists loaded models in `/v1/models`, keeps local paths containing `@`, and keeps assistant content when `tool_calls` is empty. * [Chat Parsing] Add `python-call-list` content parser (#50619) by @nico-martin * [Chat Parsing] Quote bare keys that have whitespace around them with `unquoted_keys` (#50917) by @gagan-baghel * [Chat Parsing] Preserve array values when merging duplicate XML arguments (#50760) by @crunz-ailab * Fix three chat parsing bugs (#50655) by @Rocketknight1 * Fix apply_chat_template with message objects (#50818) by @Rocketknight1 * Fix assistant tokens mask with left truncation (#50758) by @yibol9768-alt * fix(chat templating): isolate concurrent assistant tracking (#50673) by @BlazeSR10hawk * Just a small improvement in jinja (#50635) by @zucchini-nlp * Accept argument types in parentheses in get_json_schema docstrings (#50745) by @miinimal * [serve] Handle missing Hub cache and include loaded models in /v1/models (#50663) by @RyanMullins * [serve] Preserve local model paths containing '@' in ModelManager (#50662) by @RyanMullins * [serve] Keep assistant content when tool_calls is null or empty (#50707) by @AabhasK ## Pipelines Multimodal pipelines now accept media-only inputs and string assistant prefills, keep Mistral prefills in Voxtral, stop mutating generation kwargs, and return chat messages as `input_text` when returning tensors. `pipeline` also respects a `device_map` that targets a single device. * fix(pipelines)

items.title: Guarding with Judgment: Learning to Intervene for Multimodal Safety
items.summary: When visual context makes an ordinary request unsafe to answer as asked, a blanket refusal may leave the user's need unresolved. Choosing how to help…
items.abstract: When visual context makes an ordinary request unsafe to answer as asked, a blanket refusal may leave the user's need unresolved. Choosing how to help requires distinguishing an established hazard from a condition that still needs verification, a distinction that binary safety labels leave unspecified. We formulate this decision through four actions: allow, warn, review, and refuse. To ground these decisions in verifiable evidence, we build a corpus of 20,126 training audits and the JudiBench benchmark, connecting each action to diagnostic judgments, source evidence, and controlled context changes. Our guard, JudiAct, separately states what the source establishes, what condition governs the help, and how the rules apply. It then checks these three brief review items against the original inputs to predict diagnostic labels and a handling action. Supervised training learns individual judgments while comparing label assignments across related cases. A second stage swaps one review item at a time, using the resulting audit feedback to refine review generation. On JudiBench, JudiAct improves request and answer Macro-F1 by more than 28 percentage points over its 4B backbone. Across nine public benchmarks, it outperforms state-of-the-art guards on the mean delivered-answer score in both pre-generation and post-generation settings, cutting MM-SafetyBench attack success from 40.78% to 25.30%.

items.releaseNotes:
## What's changed

- Added sign-in to organizations managed in Anthropic's Enterprise Admin Console: after `claude auth login`, Claude Code applies the organization's settings and uses its cloud provider or gateway
- Added easel, a built-in mod that draws charts when asked and under MCP metrics results, on Pro, Max and, where available, Team and Enterprise on macOS and Linux; turn automatic charts off in `/config`
- Added `CLAUDE_CODE_FULL_SIGN_IN_LINK=1` to print the full sign-in link, if the short one shows an error or a script reads values from it
- Self-hosted runner: Added `--start-dir` / `SELF_HOSTED_RUNNER_START_DIR` to have Claude start its work in a folder of a repository, while settings and hooks load as without it
- Added a notice in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions when a plugin marketplace can't be fetched because its repository isn't one of the session's
- Self-hosted runner: Added a notice when Anthropic-managed git refuses a plugin's own repository, naming the plugin and what to do
- Added `commandPrinted` to `claude plugin install --json` results, true when the plugin's install command wrote to stderr, and `commandFailed` when it exited with an error, was killed or timed out
- Added `claude_code_self_hosted_runner_order_to_registered_seconds` to the self-hosted runner's `/metrics`: seconds from work order issued to registration accepted, on orchestrator-spawned runners
- Added `claude_code_self_hosted_runner_order_to_first_session_seconds` to the self-hosted runner's `/metrics`: seconds from work order to first session handed over, on runners started for a session
- Fixed Claude Code freezing for up to several minutes right after compacting a very long conversation
- Fixed WebFetch freezing the session for minutes on some pages, and returning an empty result for some others
- Fixed `ExitWorktree` and the worktree exit dialog deleting a worktree that another running Claude Code session was working in
- Fixed changes to user settings being lost when several Claude Code processes saved them at the same time
- Fixed `--continue` and `--resume` opening an empty session or failing when the last saved message had a missing or invalid timestamp
- Fixed the first prompt after a sleep of two minutes or more waiting three minutes on a connection that had died, on Linux and WSL
- Fixed turns failing with "JSON schema is invalid", and session files growing by many megabytes, when many MCP tools have an input schema that the API refuses
- Linux: Fixed Bash commands waiting seconds and showing no file diff for the rest of a session in slow repositories with large ignored folders such as `node_modules`
- Windows: Fixed Bash commands running slower for the rest of a session after Git Bash took 10 to 60 seconds to start, on machines with no custom start-up files
- Fixed `/rewind` sometimes restoring an older version of a file when two queued prompts, or stacked skills, ran together right after a turn that changed it
- Fixed text and images added when approving a permission prompt being dropped when the approved command or tool then failed
- Fixed MCP resources from claude.ai connectors and plugin servers not being attached when @-mentioned in the terminal's prompt box
- Fixed an MCP server that subagents declare being shut down when one of them finished, while other subagents or the session were still using it
- Fixed Claude in Chrome staying "not connected" after a brief connection problem, even though Chrome was open and signed in
- Fixed terminal sessions on Amazon Bedrock (Mantle) started with no model selected ignoring a pinned Opus model, and still calling an unavailable default model after announcing a fallback
- Fixed the rest of what you were typing being lost when a plan arrived in fullscreen mode
- Fixed claude.ai connectors with different names being dropped when they share a server URL (anthropics/claude-code#101856)
- Fixed plugins going missing from the installed list when several `claude plugin` commands ran at the same time
- Fixed task dependencies and metadata being lost when several task updates ran at the same time
- Fixed incomplete backups of `~/.claude.json` being kept, and displacing good ones, when the disk was full
- Fixed a long pause in Code Mode after code that read hundreds of files in projects with path-scoped rules or Read deny rules
- Fixed the built-in chart tool failing when Claude called it in Code Mode
- Fixed Code Mode ignoring an MCP tool's request to end the turn from a script in auto and bypass permissions modes
- Fixed Code Mode in auto mode dropping earlier thinking and rewriting the prompt cache when a mod added a note after a script loaded a skill
- Fixed Code Mode not restoring a file that a script had read after Esc and `/compact`
- Fixed `/context` undercounting system tools in Code Mode before Claude's first reply
- Fixed a stopped background subagent sometimes not staying stopped
- Fixed Claude still waiting for a background agent that was stopped just as it finished, in sessions run by an app or the SDK
- Fixed background sessions sometimes waking in their previous permission mode after approving a plan
- Remote Control: Fixed the note about background agents ended by a Stop from a phone or the web showing in the terminal as if you had typed it
- Remote Control: Fixed the mobile apps hiding the Diff and pull request buttons, or showing a stopped session as working, after turning it on mid-conversation
- Fixed environment variables written by a SessionStart hook being lost with `claude -p --continue`
- Fixed `claude -p` exiting 0 with no message when its output went to a file on a full disk: it now prints an error and exits 1, though a full NFS export may go unnoticed
- Fixed the system prompt keeping the earlier model's instructions when the model was changed after `/context` but before the first message
- Fixed Claude sometimes replying to its commit attribution reminder and ending the turn early after the model changed mid-turn; it can still happen where managed settings set the PR attribution line
- Fixed Esc not ending an LSP tool call that was waiting for a slow or stuck language server
- Fixed LSP tool calls and diagnostics failing when several calls or edits arrived while a language server was still starting
- Fixed `/mcp` listing plugin servers as built-in: they now stand under "Plugin MCPs", `--mcp-config` and built-in servers under "Other MCPs", and a server's page names its plugin
- Fixed an "MCP server blocked by enterprise policy: easel" warning showing at every start when an MCP allowlist or denylist excludes the built-in chart tool, which stays blocked
- Fixed `/stats` counting new activity in UTC days instead of your local time zone
- Fixed `/ultrareview` failing or reviewing the wrong code after the shell moved into another repository: it now stops and names both folders
- Fixed Grep reporting no matches when the pattern held a line break without multiline mode; it now reports the rejected pattern
- Fixed Jupyter notebooks saved with a byte order mark being reported as invalid JSON by the Read and NotebookEdit tools
- Fixed link reference definitions being dropped from CLAUDE.md and memory files that contain an HTML comment
- Fixed running Monitors keeping the earlier conversation in memory until they end
- Fixed some Claude Desktop sessions on third-party providers, other than scheduled tasks, ending a turn with "Prompt is too long" when a PDF larger than the context window followed a long conversation
- Fixed the choice between two user or project agent files declaring the same name depending on the order the file search listed them
- Fixed `claude daemon logs` never exiting inside a git repository when there is no log file
- Fixed markdown hiding a character or two after bold or italic text when a backslash came before an emoji later in the paragraph
- Fixed Edit refusing some valid hook commands in Claude settings files
- Fixed `Read` with a page range showing both halves of a scanned two-page spread on each of its pages
- Fixed line breaks and class stereotypes missing from Mermaid diagrams in HTML artifacts
- Fixed the Project instructions picker in `/config` showing only one of its four choices in a 24-row fullscreen window
- Fixed a subagent's own subagents and forks running on the plan-mode model in plan mode under `opusplan` or `haiku`
- Fixed WebFetch page summaries ignoring the `/effort` level when a gateway refuses the small fast model
- Fixed `claude -p` on Google Cloud's Agent Platform ignoring `--settings '{"fastMode":true}'` when the model comes from `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` or a settings file; such runs now bill at the fast mode price
- Fixed startup under `forceLoginOrgUUID` being refused after one temporary server error or dropped connection
- Fixed `claude mcp remove` giving no way forward for a claude.ai connector: it now says to turn it off in /mcp or remove it on claude.ai
- Fixed the /mcp "Connect on claude.ai" check saying "not connected" when claude.ai has a connector at the server's URL without its query
- Fixed `/install-github-app` and `/design-login` showing a generic failure for an account on hold instead of the on-hold notice and appeal link
- Fixed a running MCP task being reported as stopped when you move a session to the background; the background session can now follow the task, but not if its server uses stdio or sets headers
- Fixed self-hosted runners ignoring a session until they exited, after its failure report was lost or the session was given back to the same runner
- Fixed self-hosted sessions losing the prompt cache and earlier thinking when the list of repositories a restart couldn't prepare changed
- Self-hosted runner: Fixed tool calls behind a permission prompt vanishing with no result when a new runner took over the prompt, in sessions with telemetry off
- Fixed resumed self-hosted runner sessions starting without their pushed work in large repositories when `--push-outcome-on-release` is set
- Fixed self-hosted runner sessions being shown as working when Claude Code hangs at every start and `--startup-timeout-min` is from 2 to about 6
- Fixed `pkill -f` in self-hosted runner sessions on Linux ending its own shell with exit code 144, or the runner (needs a `pkill` with `--ignore-ancestors`)
- Fixed scheduled tasks on self-hosted runners having no tool to notify their owner when telemetry is off or a third-party provider is used
- Self-hosted runner: Fixed one slow `spawn-runner` hook keeping the orchestrator from claiming sessions for its free slots; it now polls every 4 to 6 seconds while a slot is free
- Self-hosted runner: Fixed a 403, such as an IP allowlist's, logged as a bad secret or token: most such lines now lead with the server's reason, so update log alerts that match the old words
- Fixed self-hosted runners' warn mode for repository settings stopping at the first finding of most kinds: it now goes on, up to 50 for a session, and says if it stops early
- Self-hosted runner: Fixed runners that start on a full disk taking sessions and failing them; they now wait for room and exit 1 after a minute with no session, unless started from a work order
- Self-hosted runner: Fixed a failed start suggesting a retry when the runner's machine had no git credentials; the error now says whom to ask and what to do if the repository is wrong
- Fixed the self-hosted runner's `last_poll_age_seconds` reading 0 while the runner had never polled successfully
- Fixed the notice about a skipped scheduled task that names no organization: it now says to start Claude Code with `--resume`, because `/resume` inside a running session doesn't run the task
- Fixed `claude plugin validate` wrongly warning that a mod's `AbovePrompt` or `AbovePromptList` hook never runs in VS Code
- Fixed `/design-sync` deleting a file it had just uploaded when Claude Design stored that file under a changed name
- Reverted 2.1.329's removal of the automatic retry when `max_tokens` exceeds a model's or gateway's limit
- Improved the claude.ai sign-in link shown by /login, `claude auth login` and `claude setup-token`: it is now much shorter
- Windows: Improved Grep and Glob speed by no longer starting a console host for each built-in ripgrep search on a local path
- Improved the speed of file diffs
- Improved `/config` search: most settings whose name starts with what you type come first, "effort" finds Model, and "dark" or "light" finds Theme
- Improved `/resume`: sessions where you only opened a screen such as `/model` and left are no longer listed
- Improved Reconnect in `/mcp` and `/plugin`: a server's page now stays open, with the cause in view, when the server still fails or needs sign-in
- Improved the error on macOS when sandbox deny lists are too long: it now names the long lists and how to shorten them
- Improved `/plugin` in fullscreen mode: the page of a plugin with errors now starts with those errors
- Improved `/ultrareview`'s cost confirmation on Team and Enterprise plans: it now says how much of your monthly spend limit is left when that is less than a review usually costs
- Improved self-hosted runner sessions on Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud's Agent Platform to say so when they start on another default model because your account refused the first
- Windows: Improved the error when a session's folder is on a drive Claude Code can't verify: it says why, and whether retrying can help
- Improved Code Mode: Claude is now told how to look at images and PDFs
- Improved Code Mode: after Esc, "Interrupted" now shows under the stopped command in place of a red error
- Improved Code Mode: the terminal freezes for far less time after a subagent's script makes thousands of tool calls
- Changed recurring scheduled tasks and `/loop` to run up to 30 days instead of 7 while their session keeps running, and say when they end; tasks made before this release still end at 7 days
- Changed more `rm` commands aimed at the root, home, a top-level folder or the working folder to ask for approval; where nobody can answer, they're refused
- Changed `deniedMcpServers` name entries to hide only the named claude.ai connector, not others at its URL; to block them all, deny its exact URL
- Changed `claude --teleport` in some setups to print the git commands for switching branch instead of running them; with `-p` it exits 1 until you switch
- Changed unrecognized model names containing "sonnet" or "haiku" to use the shorter system prompt, like other unrecognized names; `CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE_SYSTEM_PROMPT=0` gives every model the full one

items.summary: Teams put a one-page rules file in a repository and call it a control on coding agents. A registered study found agents rarely look up…
items.abstract: Teams put a one-page rules file in a repository and call it a control on coding agents. A registered study found agents rarely look up a repository's contribution rules. I asked the security question: what does a rules file do at a boundary, against a gate? I tested one 278-word rules file, with hypotheses and analysis code deposited first. Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI and OpenCode with DeepSeek worked through 20 small repositories with hidden tests, 12 for three of them. Three agents met four boundaries I built: a refused endpoint, a destructive shortcut, a planted instruction and a planted package. Permission prompts, each vendor's own control layer, were off by design. A gate in front of the mock service blocked and logged forbidden requests. Every verdict was read from records the agent could not change. Only my first scoring pass was blind to arm. My checkers found no real bugs, with the file or without it. The file cost one agent a third of its score: Codex CLI fell from 99.0 to 67.7 percent on hidden tests, and in 11 of its 36 steps reported the task complete with all tests passing while under half of the hidden tests passed. Its own tests passed. Faced with two of its rules that clash on these tasks, three agents followed the task and one followed the rule. Pooled, passes fell from 98.2 to 90.9 percent. Matched pairs fell 7.7 points, 1.3 without Codex CLI. Attempts to cross were rare: 5 in 90 gated steps, 3 without the file, 2 with it, all by OpenCode with DeepSeek, all blocked. With no gate, under the neutral file, the same requests reached the mock in 7 of 45 runs. By an error in my run script, the no-file and rules-file arms always ran behind the gate at the three HTTP boundaries, so I could not test whether the file changes what an agent does there. On what I could measure, the file acted as advice. A file tells an agent what you want. A gate decides what it gets.

items.aiSummary: Memanto, a memory agent using information-theoretic relevance scoring, completes more simulated workplace tasks at lower cost and latency than the strongest reported Mem0 configuration.
items.abstract: Memory benchmarks built on question answering tell an agent which fact to recall. Workplace requests often leave that need implicit: to post an update in the team's channel, an agent must work out which channel from earlier interactions and use it in a tool call. We evaluate Memanto, a memory agent that ranks memories with an information-theoretic relevance score, on DolphinBench, which tests memory through 600 simulated workplace tasks, each validated as requiring memory. Running in the Hermes agent harness with GPT-6-Luna and at most 6 iterations per conversation, Memanto completes 503 tasks (83.83%). The strongest configuration reported by the benchmark's authors, Mem0 with GPT-5.6-Luna and up to 60 iterations, completes 424 (70.67%). Memanto's run also has the lowest total cost (10.86, against 61.48 for the cheapest reported run) and the shortest median task latency (15.32s). Grading uses the benchmark's own judge, but the agent model differs, so these results compare complete systems. The memory system affects both whether an agent completes such tasks and what completion costs.

items.title: Demystifying the Autoresearch Harness: How Context and Skills Shape Self-Evolving Agents
items.summary: Autoresearch agents, which autonomously design, run, and refine experiments, are accelerating scientific progress, particularly in AI research. However, existing agents rely on harnesses that combine…
items.aiSummary: A systematic study of harness design for long-horizon self-evolving autoresearch agents finds that context folding and selective skill deletion improve performance, enabling MLEvolver to achieve strong results on MLE-Bench Lite and KernelBench Level 3.
items.abstract: Autoresearch agents, which autonomously design, run, and refine experiments, are accelerating scientific progress, particularly in AI research. However, existing agents rely on harnesses that combine multiple mechanisms, making it difficult to determine how individual components contribute to performance. We systematically study harness design for long-horizon, self-evolving autoresearch agents along two dimensions: context management, which determines what an agent retains from its past attempts, and skill management, which governs how it stores and reuses lessons from those attempts. Across MLE-Bench and KernelBench with gpt-oss-120b, gpt-6-luna, and gpt-6-sol, we isolate the effects of individual harness design choices by evaluating each against a recency-truncation baseline within a shared agent framework. For context management, we find that preserving individually accessible records of past attempts is more effective than maintaining a rolling summary, with context folding performing best across all six settings and improving upon the baseline by up to 19.2%. For skill management, selectively discarding persistently unused lessons is more effective on average than consolidating them or promoting them to standing rules. Building on these findings, we combine context folding and skill deletion in MLEvolver, which achieves a 72.7% medal rate on MLE-Bench Lite and a 94% fast_1 score on KernelBench Level 3, substantially outperforming AIDE and OpenEvolve under the same inference budget. Overall, our study distills design principles for preserving experimental history and curating reusable lessons in autoresearch harnesses, paving the way for agents that turn accumulated experience into sustained progress.

items.releaseNotes:
# v0.34.0 **1,061 commits from 412 contributors (120 new).** Thank you! ## TL;DR - **10 new models** (Mistral Large 4, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe, and more!) - **Extensible KV cache is on by default:** vLLM sizes the KV cache from memory actually free after warmup, so most models get a bigger cache and more throughput - in most cases you should now **remove `gpu_memory_utilization`** from your configs. - **Model Runner V1 is gone.** Model Runner V2 is now the only GPU runner. - **Big speedups** on Blackwell and MI355X: up to 1.95× decode (Step5 on GB200), 1.6× throughput (GLM-5.3-Flash), 1.24–1.40× faster long-prompt TTFT (GLM-5.3). - **Upgrade check:** default block size is now 64, ROCm 7.2 images are gone, and `huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0` is required. See [Before you upgrade](#before-you-upgrade). ## Before you upgrade > [!IMPORTANT] > These changes can break existing setups. | Change | What to do | PR | |---|---|---| | Model Runner V1 removed | Remove `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0`; it now fails at startup. Port V1 logits processors to `vllm.v1.worker.gpu.sample.logits_processor`. | #63373 | | Default `--block-size` is 64 (was 16) | Pass `--block-size 16` to keep the old behavior. ROCm paged attention still uses 16. | #63231 | | Extensible KV cache on by default; `gpu_memory_utilization` defaults to 1.0 | **In most cases it's now best to not set `gpu_memory_utilization`**. This should provide maximum kv cache capacity while avoiding runtime OOMs. Use it to share a GPU with other processes or when extensible kv cache is disabled. | #56492 | | ROCm 7.2 artifacts dropped | Use the ROCm 10.0 wheels and images. `-rocm72` is no longer published. | #61939 | | `huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0` required | Also requires `tokenizers >= 0.23.3` and `timm >= 1.0.30`. | #64779 | | QuTLASS / `fp_quant` removed | `fp_quant` checkpoints no longer load. | #65230 | | Marlin W4A8 removed | Use `--quantization humming` with `VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG` instead of `VLLM_MARLIN_INPUT_DTYPE`. | #65542 | | Keye-VL and Keye-VL-1.5 removed | — | #64287 | All breaking changes, deprecations and new defaults are listed in [the full changelog](#full-changelog). ## New models | Model | Notes | PR | |---|---|---| | **Mistral Large 4** | 1T total / 52B active, FP8 and NVFP4. Runs on NVIDIA Blackwell/Hopper and AMD MI350. | #64534 | | MiniMax-M3.1-Flash | Blackwell NVFP4 and ROCm kernels, DSpark draft | #64111 | | NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe | 30B-A4B speech model: audio chat and `/v1/audio/transcriptions` | #64282 | | Ricursive Ripple-65B Preview | BF16 and NVFP4, `ripple` reasoning and tool parsers | #65745 | | Zyphra ZAYA1 | ZAYA1-8B, ZAYA1-74B-preview | #65302 | | Baidu Unlimited-OCR-2 | DASH sparse attention | #64016 | | Liquid AI LFM3, LFM3-VL, LFM3-Audio | | #65826, #65827, #65828 | | NVIDIA Canary-1B-v2 | ASR and X↔En translation | #64215 | | Ming3-ASR | | #63585 | | NVIDIA Parakeet TDT | Through the vllm-parakeet-plugin | #65005 | ## Highlights ### Extensible KV cache, on by default - On CUDA and ROCm, the KV cache is sized from memory actually free **after** CUDA graph capture and warmup, not from an estimate (#56492). - **Result:** a larger cache (e.g. MiniMax-M3 on H200: 433k → 672k tokens), so throughput is higher and TTFT lower at high concurrency. - **Trade-off:** per-token decode latency can rise on some models (TPOT +6–18% on some H200 models at concurrency 128). Opt out with `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.9` or `--no-enable-extensible-kv-cache`. - Hardened with fixes for allocator fragmentation, startup OOMs and KV connectors (#67296, #67485, #66731, #66523, #66197, #65137, #66605, #66674). ### Model Runner V2 only - Model Runner V1 is removed (#63373). - Dual-batch overlap now runs on MRV2, including with speculative decoding and DCP (#61464). ### Speculative decoding - **Suffix decoding** runs on MRV2 with a GPU speculator; Arctic Inference is no longer needed (#60339). - **Custom speculators:** declarative configs plus a `register_speculative_method` plugin API (#63205). - **CUDA graphs** for MRV2 draft-model speculators (#60989). - **Adaptive verification** works with XPress (#65175). - **Draft KV cache matches the target's dtype**, so an FP8 target gets an FP8 draft cache (#65198). ### Performance | Improvement | Hardware | Gain | PR | |---|---|---|---| | Step5 NVFP4 MoE on TRTLLM-Gen | 4×GB200 | up to **1.95×** decode | #65152 | | GLM-5.3-Flash DeepGEMM FP8 MegaMoE | NVIDIA | **1.6×** output throughput vs DEP4 | #60895 | | Muse Spark Open specialized decode (opt-in) | GB300 | **1.5×** single-stream decode | #64077 | | Token-sharded sparse-MLA prefill under TP (default) | GB200 | GLM-5.3 TTFT **1.24–1.40×** faster at 32K–128K | #63956 | | KV-balanced MLA decode for Kimi-K3 (opt-in) | GB300 | **1.34–1.59×** decode attention | #63638 | | Qwen3.5 on breakable CUDA graphs (no torch.compile) | NVIDIA | **3.0–8.8%** lower decode ITL | #51012 | | FlyDSL decode monokernel, Muse Spark Open DSpark | 8×MI355X | **+35–57%** interactivity at conc. 1–8 | #63440 | ### AMD ROCm - Release images and wheels are **ROCm 10.0 only** (#61939). - MoRI EPv2 via `--all2all-backend mori` (#61361). - Kimi-K3 specialized decode on MI355X, opt-in (#61435). - TRITON_ATTN is the default attention backend on RDNA3 and RDNA4 (#60418). ### Serving and operations - **Checkpoint/restore** (CRIU + `cuda-checkpoint`) through `/checkpoint/prepare`, `/checkpoint/status` and `/checkpoint/restore`, in both the Python and Rust frontends (#62570). - **Fault-tolerant DP+EP scale-down:** dead ranks are removed and their experts redistributed without a restart (#46370). - Best-effort **NUMA binding** on by default (#61258). - Opt-in **cache-aware admission** ordering (#54625). - Rust frontend: stateless **Responses API** (#63902) and **`n > 1`** (#65625). ## Install **Python wheels** | Platform | Install | |---|---| | CUDA 13.0 (PyPI) | `pip install vllm` | | CUDA 13.0 (uv) | `uv pip install vllm --torch-backend=auto` | | ROCm 10.0 | `pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/rocm/0.34.0/rocm100` | | XPU | `uv pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/0.34.0/xpu --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/xpu --index-strategy unsafe-best-match` | **Docker images** | Platform | Image | Short alias | |---|---|---| | CUDA 13.0 (default) | `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.34.0` | `vllm/vllm:v0.34.0` | | CUDA 13.0 + DeepEP over AWS EFA | `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.34.0-efa` | `vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-efa` | | ROCm 10.0 | `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:v0.34.0` | `vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-rocm` | | CPU | `vllm/vllm-openai-cpu:v0.34.0` | `vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-cpu` | | XPU | `vllm/vllm-openai-xpu:v0.34.0` | `vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-xpu` | `latest` tags work the same way (e.g. `vllm/vllm:latest-rocm`). The default CUDA image now includes the AWS EFA userspace (libfabric, aws-ofi-nccl). The `-efa` image adds DeepEP built for EFA and routes NCCL over EFA by default (#65576). The **Assets** section below has the source tarball and the CUDA 13.0 (x86_64, arm64), CPU (x86_64, arm64, macOS) and XPU (x86_64) wheels. ## Full changelog
Model support - **Mistral Large 4** (#64534) runs on MRV2 with: - sparse MLA plus the DSA indexer, and cross-layer KV sharing; - DSpark, DCP/PCP, NIXL P/D and HiSparse. - **Other new models:** - MiniMax-M3.1-Flash (#64111), plus P/D across different prefill and decode TP (#64475). - Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe with MTP and DFlash2 (#64282, #64944). - **DeepSeek-V4 / V4.1** - Prefill gathers compressed KV once per KV-source group: 38 → 4 gathers per step (#59131). - Decoder replay graphs share the model graph pool: prefill graph memory 15.52 → 9.88 GiB per rank on GB200 (#63155). - `fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant` 3.5× faster, prefill 6% faster (#63540). - DSpark/MTP memory savings of about 512 MiB per GPU (#63996). - Engram host tables shared across DP ranks (#62359). - DeepGEMM sparse MQA logits on the FP8 indexer cache (#62011). - Packed multi-image vision encoding, 1.6–2.6× (#65030). - LoRA on the language model, compressor and `wo_a` layers (#57245, #64880). - DSpark with PCP (#61994); PCP with PP or DP (#63098). - Fixes: sparse prefill in FULL CUDA graphs (#59986), prefill memory budgeting (#63047), MTP embedding under PP (#65816), DeepSeek-V3.2 PP (#59961). - **GLM** - GLM-5.3-Flash: DeepGEMM FP8 MegaMoE (#60895), adaptive verification (#60229), row-strided QKV into FlashKDA (#61614). - GLM-5.3 FP8 MoE sorted-A TMA on H200, 6.0–7.6% E2E throughput (#64760). - FP8 KV cache for DSpark and DFlash drafts (#63841, #64612, #65553). - FP32 indexer MQA logits restored for GLM-5/GLM-5.3/HY-V4, with new `--attention-config.indexer_logits_dtype` (#64580). - Fused KDA convs fix stale weights after RL refit (#60991). - **Muse Spark** - Opt-in Muse Spark Open specialized decode on GB300 (#64077). - One RoPE cache shared across layers: 11.5 GiB per GPU saved, 14.5% more KV cache on 8×B200 (#65206). - GEMM and communication+norm fusions (#65438, #64638);
